tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement (thutt/build-tool-comparator README results, harness in scripts/runner.sh and scripts/build-*.sh, GPL-3.0) of Bazel against GNU Make 4.3 and Ninja 1.11.1 with tool versions, parallelism, RAM and kernel stated; CPU model is not stated, so not A. Every quoted figure matches the README tables.
notes: All claimed figures verified in the README tables (x86_64 100,000 modules: incr 61.911 vs 692.201/292.019 s, NULL 20.193 vs 688.101/285.583 s; 5,000 modules: incr 4.040 vs 22.408/24.813 s; Ninja and no-builtin-rules Make rows also match). Weak entry: the benchmark repo has 5 stars and its author is openly Bazel-sceptical; Bazel wins only against default-rules Make on incremental/null builds at scale, loses to Ninja in every row and to Make -rR, and its full builds are slowest everywhere. Orchestrator may weigh whether default-rules Make counts as a crippled baseline; it is the out-of-the-box Make configuration and the benchmark applies out-of-the-box settings to every tool.

tier_reason: Measurement by the Meson author (not a Ninja author) in mesonbuild/meson docs/markdown/Simple-comparison.md, comparing CMake's Make backend with its Ninja backend; generator and measurement scripts are public (linked gen_src.py, measure.py) and the build type and -j 4 are stated, but compiler version and CPU model are not, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Page text: switching the CMake backend from Make to Ninja shaves 3.5 seconds (over 20%) off the total build time of the 1000-file project with no CMake file changes. Chart values (bar-chart PNGs, read off approximately): full build CMake/Make about 16 s vs CMake/Ninja about 12.5 s; empty (no-op) build CMake/Make about 0.55 s vs CMake/Ninja about 0.04 s (about 13x, derived from page data). Page text also says Meson (Ninja backend) takes 0.03 s for the empty build and Autotools, the fastest Make-based system, is almost an order of magnitude slower. Anecdote on the same page: no-op build times of 30 seconds for Make versus less than one second for Ninja when compiling the Clang compiler.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Linked measure.py: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=debug (default Unix Makefiles generator) then make -j 4, versus cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=debug -G Ninja then ninja -j 4; system C compiler picked by CMake (the Meson row sets CC=gcc); compiler, CMake, Make and Ninja versions are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The only quantified third-party comparison reachable is written by the author of Meson, a meta-build system that itself generates Ninja files (an interested party for Ninja, competing with CMake rather than with Ninja), and is old (2011-era MacBook Pro, Ubuntu 13.04). CPU model, compiler and tool versions are not stated. The generator and measurement scripts are linked from the page (raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/jpakkane/meson/gen_src.py and measure.py); measure.py times a single build and a single empty build per tool, while the page says the fastest of several runs was taken. The per-tool values are in bar-chart PNGs, so the figures other than the 3.5 s / over 20% text are read off the charts and approximate. The baseline is CMake-generated Makefiles, not a hand-written Makefile, so the gap partly reflects CMake's Makefile generator. The 30 s versus under 1 s Clang figure is explicitly anecdotal. First-party claim on the Ninja manual page (https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/blob/master/doc/manual.asciidoc, introduction): Chromium, with over 30,000 source files, had other build systems, including one built from custom non-recursive Makefiles, that took ten seconds to start building after changing one file, while Ninja takes under a second; no hardware, date or method is given there, so it is tier C on its own. Ninja's advantage is mostly incremental and no-op startup time; clean full builds are compiler-bound, and the 20 percent gain is on a synthetic project of trivial files, so real projects will see less on clean builds.

notes: Page text figures confirmed; the record wrongly said the generator script is absent and that the charts were unreadable (both PNGs fetched and read). Meson is not a competitor of Ninja (it uses Ninja as its backend), so caveats reworded. Tier B kept as independent-of-Ninja measurement with public scripts; it is old and modest evidence.

tier_reason: First-party benchmark (cpp-testing/ut-benchmark, linked from the UT README as its benchmark) with public code (benchmarks/bench.sh, Makefile) and stated compilers and flags (clang++ with gcc 9.2.0 toolchain, g++, -std=c++2a, -g, -O3 -DNDEBUG), but no CPU model or machine, so not A; first-party, so C.

corrections.caveats: Numbers come only from bar-chart PNGs in the benchmark repo (no tables), so every figure above is read off a chart and approximate. The CPU model and machine are not stated anywhere, so the run falls short of tier A. The benchmark repo (cpp-testing/ut-benchmark, 13 stars, no license file) is the UT README's own linked benchmark, i.e. first-party. Versions are from 2019 (UT 1.1.0, GoogleTest 1.10.0, Catch2 2.10.2, doctest 2.3.5, Boost.Test 1.71.0, gcc 9 and clang 9); UT itself is now at 2.x and newer releases of every framework exist and were not re-measured. On the large suite+assert+stl workload doctest matches or beats UT: about 50 s vs 55 s with clang9 default, about equal with gcc9 default and -g (about 80 s and 88 s each), and clearly faster with clang9 -O3 (about 145 s vs 215 s); only with gcc9 -O3 is UT ahead (about 230 s vs 270 s). UT's compile-time lead is clear against Boost.Test, GoogleTest and Catch2 and mixed against doctest; on the include-only and 1,000-test single-file workloads UT leads all frameworks including doctest. The '5x faster because it does not introduce a new type for each lambda' line is a code comment in the README's implementation section, a design claim with no benchmark behind it. UT's own test registration style differs from the baselines, so workloads are not byte-identical test programs.

notes: All chart readings in claimed_speedup checked against the PNGs and match. Added the clang9 -O3 suite row where doctest compiles faster than UT. Category compile-caching-and-distribution is a loose fit for a unit-testing framework whose claim is faster compile of test code; orchestrator may want a category override.
